edge_951.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, and the frontierism Canadian historians took from it, criticised as environmental determinism; the frontier recast as a dependent of the metropolis (1954)
edge_951.evidence_note: His own words. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954), read in full. He summarises Turner's thesis that 'the greatest formative influence' in American history had been 'the open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6) and judges: 'This was environmental determinism at its most forthright. The wilderness and the men it produced had made America' (p. 7). Against it he sets the metropolitan reading: the frontier's culture 'originally stems from a metropolitan community; at root, learning and ideas radiate from there—and thus is Turner answered' (p. 18); 'the frontier, far from being essentially independent and self-reliant, is in the largest sense a dependent' (p. 18); and 'the functioning of metropolitanism may do more to explain the course of Canadian history than concepts of frontierism borrowed from the United States and set forth before the significance of the modern metropolis was clear' (p. 20). 'At any rate, frontierism, along with earlier schools and approaches, has had its use and its day' (p. 21). His qualifications are kept: 'Defenders of Turner might claim that he had not proposed a frontier hypothesis as the only key to American history' (p. 7); the frontier thesis 'proper' was never 'adopted as fully or dogmatically in Canada as it was in the United States—and there, of course, it has long been the subject of qualification and criticism' (p. 1); Canadian environmentalists took over 'the general approach and mood of Turner and company ... rather than the precise frontier thesis, which received little direct application in Canada' (p. 6). He draws on American critics of Turner (Hayes, Fox, Schlesinger Jr.; pp. 7–8) and on Canadian ones (McDougall 1929, Stanley 1940; p. 10, n. 21). The critique is therefore aimed at Turner's thesis and above all at its Canadian adaptation; the Canadian historians he names sit in cdn_national_tradition and are covered by edge 1. In-period reading: Davis (1985, p. 95, read) calls the article 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'. Davis (p. 109) also quotes Careless on television saying of Turner's thesis that 'like any view of history which gets oversimplified, overpopularized, it becomes untrue; it becomes a myth' (undated, a quoted-in witness). No reply by a Turnerian historian was found or read.

edge_957.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
edge_957.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.

edge_1137.relationship: Tony Judt: The Age of Extremes keeps the categories of the 1930s, gives Bolshevism “no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms”, devotes “just six pages” to “real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia and neglects nationalism (1995)
edge_1137.evidence_note: A named reader without a node, drawn from political history because his charge concerns the book's political history. Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
edge_1137.map_label: Judt on The Age of Extremes, 1995

w2_hob_judt_1995.title: Tony Judt, “Downhill All the Way,” New York Review of Books, 25 May 1995; review of Eric Hobsbawm, The Age of Extremes: A History of the World, 1914–1991 (Pantheon, 1994).
w2_hob_judt_1995.citation: Tony Judt, “Downhill All the Way,” New York Review of Books, 25 May 1995; review of Eric Hobsbawm, The Age of Extremes: A History of the World, 1914–1991 (Pantheon, 1994).

verification.note: Complete text and endnotes read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). A "Hobsbawm generation" of historians who began between about 1959 and 1975; Primitive Rebels "first appeared in 1959"; Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation"; The Age of Revolution 1962, The Age of Capital 1975 ("Hobsbawm’s single greatest work"), The Age of Empire twelve years later. Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one" who "mostly avoids military or political narrative"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (endnote 2 defends the European focus). The "one" defect: "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject". Verdict: "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
